concepts.title: Introduction to Homographies
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a general geometric image transformation that maps pixels between views when the scene is planar or the camera only rotates.
concepts.content:
A homography is a general geometric image transformation that relates corresponding points across two images. While general viewpoints require 3D scene structure and relative camera motion to find a mapping, a simple transformation exists in specific scenarios: when the scene is planar or when two cameras are related only by a rotation. In these cases, the coordinates of corresponding points are related by a homography.

[FIGURE:d89ebe83f072de38 | A photograph of a row of academic books on a shelf, focusing on titles related to computer vision and perception. The books are arranged vertically, showing their spines with titles such as 'The...]

[FIGURE:4c2d17b07db71aed | A photograph of a bookshelf containing several academic books related to computer vision and perception. Visible titles include 'Perception as Bayesian Inference', 'The Retina', 'Foundations of...]

These two images are (approximately) related by a homography. Homographies are used in applications such as perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, creating bird's-eye views, and correcting keystone distortions.
concepts.motivation_md: Mapping one image to another usually requires complex 3D information. Homographies provide a powerful shortcut for common tasks like panoramic stitching or document scanning where the geometry is constrained.
concepts.recap_md: - Homographies relate views when the scene is flat or the camera rotation is the only change.

concepts.title: Definition of Homography
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines and can be represented by a 3x3 matrix in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
A homography (or projective transformation) is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines. It is a function $h$ that maps points such that if $\mathbf{p}_1$, $\mathbf{p}_2$, and $\mathbf{p}_3$ are colinear, their transformed points are also colinear. In homogeneous coordinates, this mapping $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$ is written as a product with a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{H}$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This is expressed in short form as $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$. In a general homography, angles and lengths are not preserved; parallel lines might not remain parallel, and lines of identical length might change. (see figure: Homography. Colinear points remain colinear after transformation. Angles between lines are not preserved.)
concepts.motivation_md: To mathematically manipulate images for tasks like perspective correction, we need a formal definition of how points move. The homography provides a linear representation (in homogeneous space) for these non-linear 2D projections.
concepts.recap_md: - A homography maps points to points while maintaining collinearity.

concepts.title: Collinearity Preservation of Homographies
concepts.one_liner: Colinear points remain colinear after a homography transformation, as shown by the transformation of the line equation in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content: To prove that colinear points remain colinear after the homography, we use the equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates, $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$. Given the homography relationship $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$, we have $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$. Substituting this into the line equation yields $(\mathbf{H}^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$, which is the equation of a line for the projected points $\mathbf{p}'$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem confirms the fundamental property of homographies: they are projective transformations that preserve the 'straightness' of lines, which is critical for maintaining the structure of objects in warped images.
concepts.recap_md: - The transformation of a line equation under a homography results in a new line equation.

concepts.title: Homography from Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: When a camera rotates around its center without translation, the mapping between corresponding points in different views is a homography.
concepts.content:
When images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera with no translation, the coordinates of corresponding points across pairs of images are related by a homography, regardless of their distance from the camera.

[FIGURE:1db46673e5bbe185 | A photograph of the Stata Center at MIT, taken at a tilted angle...]
[FIGURE:8267e250a2c64ddf | A photograph of the Stata Center at MIT, featuring complex, non-rectilinear architecture...]
[FIGURE:83ad2f9f3b5c333e | A photograph of a modern brick and metal building with complex, non-orthogonal geometry...]

As shown in (see figure: Camera rotation generates two images related by a homography.), we align the world coordinate system with camera 1. The projection of a 3D point $\mathbf{P}$ into camera 1 (with zero translation) is $\lambda_1 [x, y, 1]^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{K} [X, Y, Z]^\mathsf{T}$. For camera 2, with rotation $\mathbf{R}$, the projection is $\lambda_2 [x', y', 1]^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} [X, Y, Z]^\mathsf{T}$.

Inverting these equations to relate the common 3D point yields:
$$\begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix} = \lambda_1 \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \lambda_2 \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This establishes the relationship:
$$\lambda_2 / \lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Thus, $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$ is the $3\times3$ homography matrix relating the views. This holds even if the cameras have different intrinsic parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle is the foundation of panoramic image stitching. Because the transformation depends only on camera rotation and not on the depth of objects, we can perfectly align images taken from a tripod even if the scene has complex 3D structure.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure camera rotation creates a homography $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{K}_2 \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}_1^{-1}$.

concepts.title: Homography from Planar Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points on that plane are related by a homography.
concepts.content:
When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points inside that plane are related by a homography. This is illustrated in [FIGURE:8d12e88a6496cd81 | A photograph of a stone building facade...] and [FIGURE:d33152acf9add1c2 | A photograph of a stone building facade...], where points on a building facade are related across views.

To prove this, we place the world-coordinate system on the plane such that $Z=0$, as shown in (see figure: Geometry of a the projection of a planar scene.). The projection equation is:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Setting $Z=0$ and letting $\mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2$ be the first two columns of the rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$, we get:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This shows that points on the plane are related to image points by a homography. Since this holds for any camera, the relationship between corresponding points across two cameras for a planar scene is also a homography. While the epipolar constraint always holds, the homography is a stronger constraint that applies specifically to these planar conditions.
concepts.motivation_md: Many man-made environments consist of flat surfaces like walls or floors. Recognizing that these surfaces follow a homography allows for specialized processing, such as rectifying a perspective view of a document into a flat, top-down image.
concepts.recap_md: - Points on a 3D plane map to 2D image points via a homography matrix.

concepts.title: Image Stitching and Panoramas
concepts.one_liner: Image stitching creates large panoramas by combining multiple pictures taken by a rotating camera without translation.
concepts.content: To create a large panorama from multiple pictures, the images need to be taken by a rotating camera without translation. To stitch together images, one needs to estimate the homography relating the images to be combined. While one could estimate the rotation and intrinsic camera matrices to compute the homography, it is usually simpler to use feature correspondences. For example, initial correspondences between each pair of images can be computed using speeded up robust features (SURF). (see figure: Two overlapping images and some found correspondences using SURF descriptors. A random set of four correspondences are highlighted.)
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows for the creation of wide-angle panoramic views that exceed the field of view of a single camera shot by combining multiple overlapping images into a single seamless frame.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image stitching creates panoramas from multiple photos taken by a rotating camera without translation.
 - The process involves estimating the homography that relates overlapping image pairs.
 - Feature descriptors like SURF are used to find the initial point correspondences needed for estimation.

concepts.title: Direct Linear Transform (DLT) for Homography
concepts.one_liner: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) algorithm estimates the homography matrix relating point correspondences across two camera views using a linear system of equations.
concepts.content: Given a set of point locations and their correspondences across two cameras, we can compute the homography relating the locations of imaged points using the direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm. This provides a linear set of equations for the parameters of the homography matrix in the form: $$\mathbf{A} 	ext{h} = \mathbf{0}$$ where $\mathbf{A}$ is a $2N \times 9$ matrix when given $N$ corresponding pairs. The vector $\mathbf{h}$ contains all the elements of the matrix $\mathbf{H}$ stacked as a column vector of length 9. Note that $\mathbf{h}$ only has 8 degrees of freedom as the results do not change for a global scaling of all the values. Therefore, we need at least four correspondences to estimate the homography between two sets of corresponding points. The solution is the vector that minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$, given by the eigenvector of the matrix $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$ with the smallest eigenvalue. In practice, it is useful to also minimize the reprojection error after initializing with the DLT solution.
concepts.motivation_md: DLT provides a mathematically straightforward way to solve for the homography matrix from point matches, serving as a necessary initialization step for more complex geometric optimizations.
concepts.recap_md:
- DLT solves for the homography matrix $\mathbf{H}$ using the linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$.
 - At least four point correspondences are required to solve for the 8 degrees of freedom in the homography.
 - The optimal linear solution is the eigenvector corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$.

concepts.title: RANSAC (Random Sampling with Consensus)
concepts.one_liner: RANSAC is a robust model-fitting algorithm that estimates parameters by iteratively sampling random subsets of data and identifying the set with the most consensus inliers.
concepts.content: Random sampling with consensus (RANSAC) is an algorithm used to fit models to data robustly, especially when feature point detection is noisy or contains mismatches. The procedure is simple: first, randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of a model, such as a line or a homography. Second, compute the model parameters from that randomly sampled set. Third, compute the inliers in the dataset—the datapoints that fit the model to within some tolerance. Repeat this procedure $N$ times. Finally, compute a model from the set of inlier points corresponding to the largest number of inlier datapoints. (see figure: RANSAC applied to robust estimation of line parameters. (a) Datapoints for which robust line estimation is sought. (b) Two points (in blue) are selected at random, sufficient to estimate line model...)
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world data often contains outliers or incorrect matches that would skew standard least-squares estimates; RANSAC ignores these outliers to find the true underlying model.
concepts.recap_md:
- RANSAC iteratively selects random minimal subsets of data to propose model candidates.
 - It identifies "inliers" that agree with the proposed model within a given tolerance $\epsilon$.
 - The final model is refined using the largest set of inliers found across all iterations.

concepts.title: RANSAC Iteration Heuristic
concepts.one_liner: The RANSAC iteration heuristic determines the number of trials $k$ needed to find a good model fit with a desired probability $p$ based on the expected outlier ratio.
concepts.content: A heuristic for the number of samples $S$ required to be assured a good model fit can be derived. Let $n$ be the number of datapoints required to specify the model, and let $w$ be the probability that any selected datapoint is an inlier. The probability that all selected points are inliers is $w^n$, and the probability that at least one selected point is an outlier is $1 - w^n$. The probability that in $k$ trials only bad models are selected is $(1 - w^n)^k$. If $p$ is the probability of selecting the correct model, we have $1-p = (1 - w^n)^k$. Solving for $k$, the number of RANSAC iterations required to find a good fit with probability $p$ is: $$k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$$ In practice, points should be selected without replacement to avoid degenerate fits, though this analysis assumes selection with replacement, which is legitimate when the number of points selected is small relative to the available set.
concepts.motivation_md: Since RANSAC is a randomized algorithm, this heuristic provides a statistical guarantee on how many iterations are necessary to ensure the algorithm succeeds with high confidence.
concepts.recap_md:
- The number of iterations $k$ depends on the desired confidence $p$ and the estimated inlier ratio $w$.
 - The formula $k = \log(1-p) / \log(1-w^n)$ calculates the trials needed to pick at least one all-inlier set.
 - This heuristic assumes selection with replacement, which is valid for small sample sizes relative to the dataset.

concepts.title: Image Stitching via Homography
concepts.one_liner: Image stitching uses DLT and RANSAC to compute homographies between image pairs and warp them into a single reference coordinate system.
concepts.content: Using DLT and RANSAC, we can compute the homography between each pair of images and align them with respect to a reference image. In practice, a middle image is often chosen as the reference. We can use the estimated homographies to warp all of the images into a single camera view to create a composite panorama. (see figure: Panoramic image composed by the three overlapping images from @fig-example_three_images)
concepts.motivation_md: This concept integrates point matching, robust estimation, and geometric warping to solve the practical problem of creating seamless wide-field-of-view images from standard photos.
concepts.recap_md:
- DLT and RANSAC are combined to find robust homography matrices between overlapping photos.
 - Images are aligned by warping them into the coordinate frame of a chosen reference image.
 - The final result is a single panoramic view synthesized from multiple individual captures.
